body:
Particle process shader cannot store much state. That's why it doesn't accumulate rotation. Instead, it calculates it every frame via lifetime and current velocity. So at any given moment the velocity value is treated as if it was constant over the entire lifetime. This results in the behavior you see, but it's totally expected. Accumulating rotation would require storing more persistent per particle state data which is likely not optimal.
If you want to animate rotation over time, better to drive the rotation directly instead through angular velocity.

Interesting... This definitely helps me understand why the angular velocity curve behaves the way it does, but I'm still not convinced that this behavior makes sense. At the very least, it's inconsistent with how directional velocity is animated:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6e1be167-107b-4a40-a1d1-43484753f328

Using the same logic (i.e., calculating position based on lifetime and current velocity along the curve), I would expect these particles to move forwards and then turn around and head back to their starting point. As you can see, that is not what happens. (And I think that makes sense. After all, the goal is to animate velocity smoothly over the lifetime of the particle, not guess where it should be based on the current velocity each frame).

I am not sure exactly how these properties are implemented, but it seems to me that rotation can be derived more accurately from the velocity curve by using the area under the curve up to the current x-coordinate instead of just the angular velocity at that coordinate. This is basic calculus and shouldn't be too difficult to implement, even if the area under the curve has to be estimated using the baked points in the curve.

Thank you for the further explanation. I took some time to look through the shader code, and I think I understand what you're saying now. Correct me if I'm wrong, but the main reason that animated directional velocity behaves as expected is that position can easily be extracted and accumulated using each particle's persistent transformation matrix, like so:
`TRANSFORM[3].xyz += final_velocity * DELTA;`

As you mentioned, a similar effect could be achieved for angular velocity by extracting rotation from the matrix. I assume this isn't performed already because the process is a bit more involved and has to account for other transformations like scale and shearing along the way. Still, I don't see any reason why it wouldn't be possible to implement.

If the performance of these operations is the primary concern, then an alternative solution would be to add another built-in for particle rotation. Of course, the tradeoff here is additional memory usage per particle.

Regardless, I stand by my initial assessment that the way angular velocity curves are currently implemented is unintuitive and generally not very helpful. What is the logical next step for this issue? Does it make sense to create a separate post describing a feature proposal? You mentioned that people have complained about this before. Are there other issues that were created on this topic that I missed and should weigh in on?

@bmorledge-hampton19 Yeah, that's correct. 

The behavior indeed does seem "broken" from the perspective of an average user. Implementing the "proper" behavior is certainly possible. Hopefully there won't be some interference with other stuff that might change the rotation. There's plenty of moving part in the particle process material/shader that could affect each other.

The next step would be bringing this to attention of the developer who implemented it. Not sure there's more you can do than posting here. I'm just a regular user like yourself. If the developer engages here and explains why it was done like this - it would be ideal. 

Other than that you can try to implement it yourself in the source code and make a pull request. I might even be tempted to look into it if I get time.
